summary: Defines a SIP event package that lets a user subscribe to another user and receive notifications when the state of that user's INVITE-initiated dialogs changes. It also defines the data format used in the notifications. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine being able to ask a friend's phone to tell you whenever they start or finish a call. This memo describes how to ask and how the phone replies.

questions: how to watch call state in sip
what is the sip dialog event package
subtitle: How one SIP device can watch another user's calls start, ring, connect and end, and what the XML notifications look like.

tldr.problem: Some SIP applications, such as automatic callback or presence-aware conferencing, need to know the state of a user's calls, but the application does not sit on the user's phone or in the call path.
tldr.mechanism: A subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE for the event package named dialog, and the notifier answers with NOTIFY requests carrying an XML dialog information document. A defined dialog state machine decides when to notify and what to report.
tldr.outcome: The package, its XML format and two new feature tags (sip.byeless and sip.rendering) are a Proposed Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 7463 and RFC 8996.

facts.label: Default duration
facts.value: 2 hours for specific dialogs, 1 hour for all dialogs

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: Not faster than once every 1 second (RECOMMENDED)

today: RFC 4235 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7463 and RFC 8996, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Watch Dialog State
sections.content:
The SIP Events framework (RFC 3265) lets one party subscribe to events and receive notifications. A specific set of events is called a package. This RFC defines a package for INVITE-initiated dialogs, the SIP relationship between two peers that a call creates.

The RFC lists applications that need this knowledge. In Automatic Callback, user A calls busy user B and wants to be called back when B hangs up. In Presence-Enabled Conferencing, a server creates a call when A, B and C are all online and not on a call. In IM Conference Alerts, a phone receives an instant message when someone joins a conference it is part of.

The common thread: the application needs dialog state but is not on the end user's device. Using the package, such applications can be distributed. The RFC also adds two callee capability feature parameters, covered later.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a helper program needs to know whether you are on the phone, but it is not sitting next to you. This lets it ask your phone and get told when things change.

sections.title: The Dialog Event Package
sections.content:
The package name is dialog, carried in the Event and Allow-Events header fields. It defines four parameters: call-id, to-tag, from-tag and include-session-description. To subscribe to one specific dialog, the first three MUST be present. To subscribe to the dialogs created by a single INVITE, call-id and to-tag MUST be present.

A SUBSCRIBE may carry a body that defines a filter, but filter documents are not specified here. Without a body, the default policy applies: notify on every change of matching dialogs, or of all dialogs of the user if no identifiers were given. A dialog whose remote target matches the subscriber's own Contact is suppressed, since the subscriber is already a party to it. Session descriptions are left out unless explicitly requested and authorized.

Clients SHOULD give an explicit duration. For specific dialogs the RFC recommends a default of two hours; for all dialogs of a user the default is one hour. Notifications carry an application/dialog-info+xml document, which all subscribers and notifiers MUST support.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the phone which calls you care about, or just say all of them. If you say nothing special, it sends a note whenever anything changes, and it skips calls you are already in.

sections.title: The Dialog State Machine
sections.content:
SIP does not explicitly model dialog lifecycle, so this RFC defines a finite state machine used for both caller (UAC) and callee (UAS). It extends the usual dialog states back to the moment an INVITE is sent, so forking is handled.

The machine starts in Trying when the INVITE is sent or received. A 1xx response without a tag moves it to Proceeding; a 1xx with a tag moves it to Early; a 2xx moves it to Confirmed. If another 1xx or 2xx arrives with a different tag, a new machine instance is created, so forking produces several machines.

The machine ends in Terminated, with an event naming the cause. cancelled follows a CANCEL and a 487, rejected a non-2xx final response, and replaced a new invitation with a Replaces header. From Confirmed, local-bye and remote-bye follow a BYE, error follows a 481 or 408 to a mid-dialog request, and timeout follows no response at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A call goes through steps: dialing, ringing, talking, finished. The phone keeps track of which step each call is on and writes down why it ended.

sections.title: Notifying and Authorizing
sections.content:
Dialog information is sensitive, so all subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and then authorized. Implementors MUST support digest authentication as a baseline; the policy itself is up to the administrator. The notifier MAY send a NOTIFY on any transition of the state machine, and SHOULD send one when dialog characteristics such as Contact URIs or session descriptions change.

For an unauthenticated or third-party subscriber, the RFC recommends forbidding subscriptions to individual dialogs and permitting only subscriptions to all dialogs, answered with a single virtual state machine that reveals no dialog identifiers. The subscriber learns only that a call exists, the same as it would learn from an INVITE answered with 486 (Busy Here). In the absence of preference, Confirmed is recommended for the virtual machine. A subscriber authenticated as the same address-of-record as the user agent SHOULD get complete information, which supports shared-line phones.

Notifications normally carry only the dialogs that changed. The exceptions are a NOTIFY answering a SUBSCRIBE and one with no dialog elements, which carry the full view. Servers SHOULD NOT notify one subscriber faster than once every 1 second. A SUBSCRIBE may fork and install several subscriptions, and subscribers MUST be ready for that.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone does not tell strangers everything. A stranger may only learn that you are busy, while your own other phones can see all the details.

sections.title: The Dialog Information Document
sections.content:
The document is well-formed XML 1.0, encoded in UTF-8, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dialog-info. The root dialog-info element has three mandatory attributes: version (starts at 0 and rises by one per document sent to a subscriber), state (full or partial) and entity (the observed user).

Inside are zero or more dialog elements. Each has a mandatory id, optional call-id, local-tag, remote-tag and direction (initiator or recipient), and a mandatory state sub-element. Optional sub-elements include duration (seconds since the machine was created), replaces, referred-by, and local and remote elements holding identity, target and session-description.

A subscriber keeps a table of dialogs keyed by id. A full document flushes and repopulates the table; a partial one updates rows. A version one higher than the local one is processed. A larger jump is also processed, but if the document was partial the subscriber SHOULD send a refresh SUBSCRIBE to get full state. A lower version is discarded. Terminated rows MAY be removed at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note is a small form with a number on top. If you miss a number, you ask for a fresh full copy. If an old note shows up late, you throw it away.

sections.title: New Feature Parameters
sections.content:
Two new media feature parameters are defined, useful as input to presence, conferencing and shared-line applications. Per RFC 3840 a + prefix is used when they appear in a Contact header field.

sip.byeless is a boolean saying the user agent cannot end sessions itself. Examples given are continuous announcement services, certain recording services and call centers configured never to hang up on callers.

sip.rendering is a string saying whether the user agent is currently rendering media it receives. Its legal values are yes, no and unknown; unknown may apply to a third party call control controller. It MUST only be used in a Contact header field of a dialog created by INVITE. The RFC's shared-line example uses it to show a call placed on hold.
sections.plainLanguage: These are two little name tags a phone can wear. One says it never hangs up by itself, and the other says whether it is actually playing the sound.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
Dialog state reveals sensitive information, so the RFC relies on authentication and authorization of subscriptions and on the authorization guidelines above. All implementations MUST support digest authentication. Notifications are sensitive too, so end-to-end S/MIME encryption MAY protect them, and user agents implementing the package SHOULD also implement SIP over TLS and the sips: scheme.

The two feature tags could be abused. An attacker who can change them might alter application behavior, for example making a conferencing application end a call early. Applications using them SHOULD ensure integrity, and conveying protocols SHOULD guarantee authenticity.

The IANA section registers the application/dialog-info+xml MIME type, the XML namespace, a schema, and the two feature tags with ASN.1 identifiers 19 (sip.byeless) and 20 (sip.rendering).
sections.plainLanguage: What your phone is doing is private, so it checks who is asking before it answers. The little name tags also have to be trustworthy, or someone could trick a program.

viz.caption: TERMINATION EVENTS ALLOWED IN THE STATE ELEMENT

items.label: Cancelled
items.desc: The caller sent CANCEL and the INVITE got a 487.

items.label: Rejected
items.desc: The INVITE ended with a non-2xx final response.

items.label: Replaced
items.desc: A new invitation with a Replaces header replaced this dialog.

items.label: Local BYE
items.desc: The observed user sent a BYE.

items.label: Remote BYE
items.desc: The observed user received a BYE.

items.label: Error
items.desc: A mid-dialog request got a 481 or 408 response.

items.label: Timeout
items.desc: A mid-dialog request got no response.
